title: Quality indicators and the business case
blurb: Explain what quality indicators are and how they trace back to the business case and success criteria, so quality is defined by what delivers the benefits.
question: An online retailer's business case for a new website promises fewer product returns. The design agency proposes judging quality by 'number of award nominations'. Why is that a poor quality indicator, and how should the project choose better ones?

teach.h: Quality indicators: the gauges on the dashboard
teach.body: Quality indicators are measurable signs that the outputs are of the required quality: for example defect rates, test pass rates or customer satisfaction scores. They are derived from the business case and the success criteria, so quality is defined by what delivers the benefits. In plain English: decide why the project exists, then choose the few measurements that tell you whether the outputs will actually deliver that.

teach.caption: Every indicator should answer 'which benefit does this protect?'. If nothing in the business case needs it, question why you're measuring it.

teach.h: Why indicators must come from the business case
teach.body: The business case is the baseline that justifies the project: everything is measured against it. If quality indicators are chosen because they're easy to count or look impressive, the project can hit every target and still miss the benefits. Too strict, and you gold-plate: extra cost the benefits don't need. Too loose, and outputs aren't good enough to realise the benefits. And if the business case changes, the indicators must be reviewed too.

teach.h: Five terms the exam likes to mix up
head: Term
What it is
Retailer example
rows: Measures that judge if the project succeeded
Conditions that make success more likely
Measures tracked during the project against the criteria
Measurable signs outputs are of the required quality
Conditions a deliverable must meet to be accepted
All size guides match supplier data
teach.caption: Success criteria are agreed up front. Indicators and KPIs give evidence along the way that you're heading for them.

teach.h: Illustrative quality indicators for the retailer

items.label: product pages with an error (defect rate)

teach.caption: Scenario targets only, not standard figures. Each one links to a benefit: fewer returns, more completed sales.

teach.body: Northgate's business case says wrong sizes and missing details drive costly returns, and slow checkout loses sales. So the success criteria are a lower returns rate and a higher conversion rate. The project manager agrees indicators that predict those: product-page error rate, size-guide accuracy, customer ratings of descriptions and checkout availability. The agency's 'award nominations' is dropped: it protects no benefit. The indicators go into the quality management plan and are reported to the sponsor.

teach.caption: Several indicators can protect one benefit. Each needs a target, a measure, an owner and a frequency.

rows.label: Measured

rows.label: Feedback

rows.label: If off target

teach.text: Two traps. (1) Indicators are NOT chosen because they're easy to count or sound impressive: they are derived from the business case and success criteria. (2) Success CRITERIA measure whether the project succeeded; success FACTORS are the conditions (like an engaged sponsor) that make success more likely. Don't swap them.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define quality indicators: measurable signs of quality, such as defect rates, test pass rates, customer satisfaction.
Explain the link: they are derived from the business case and success criteria, so quality is defined by what delivers the benefits.
Say why it matters: avoids gold plating and under-delivery, keeps quality aligned to the justification.
Show use: recorded in the quality plan, measured through quality control, reported to the sponsor.
Add that indicators are reviewed if the business case changes, and compare linear and iterative if asked.
Quality indicators are measurable signs of quality: defect rates, test pass rates, customer satisfaction.
They are derived from the business case and success criteria.
So quality is defined by what delivers the benefits: no more, no less.
Success criteria judge success; success factors make it likely; KPIs track progress during the project.
Review the indicators whenever the business case changes.

summary: You can now explain what quality indicators are and trace them back through the success criteria to the business case. You can also tell success criteria, success factors, KPIs and acceptance criteria apart, and explain why indicators must change if the business case does.

A.q: Which of the following is an example of a quality indicator?
options: An engaged and supportive sponsor
Percentage of tests passed first time
The approved budget for the test phase
A stable team with specialist skills
A.why: A test pass rate is a measurable sign of the quality of the outputs, so it is a quality indicator.

whyNot.0: An engaged sponsor is a success factor: a condition that makes success more likely.
whyNot.2: A budget is a cost constraint, not a measure of output quality.
whyNot.3: A skilled, stable team is a success factor, not a measure of quality.

A.q: Quality indicators should be derived MAINLY from which source?
options: The supplier's standard test scripts
Measures that are quickest to collect
The previous project's progress reports
The business case and success criteria
A.why: Quality indicators are derived from the business case and success criteria, so quality is defined by what delivers the benefits.

whyNot.0: Supplier scripts may not reflect this project's benefits or users.
whyNot.1: Ease of collection is a poor reason: easy measures may not predict the benefits.
whyNot.2: Another project's reports reflect a different business case.

A.q: What does it mean to say that 'quality is defined by what delivers the benefits'?
options: Outputs need just the quality that the benefits require
Outputs should always use the highest specification on offer
Quality is judged only after the benefits have been realised
Benefits matter more than quality, so checks can be reduced
A.why: The required quality is set by what the business case needs: enough to realise the benefits, without gold plating.

whyNot.1: Exceeding what the benefits need is gold plating, adding cost without value.
whyNot.2: Quality is checked throughout delivery, not only after benefits are realised.
whyNot.3: Quality is how the benefits are protected; reducing checks puts them at risk.

B.q: An airline's business case for new self-service bag drops is based on cutting check-in queue times. Which quality indicator is MOST relevant?
options: Number of colours available for the kiosk casing
Number of team members trained in the agile method
Average time for a passenger to drop a bag unaided
Number of design documents produced by the supplier
B.why: Bag-drop time directly predicts the benefit in the business case: shorter queues.

whyNot.0: Casing colours don't affect queue times, so this protects no benefit.
whyNot.1: Team training is a success factor, not a measure of output quality.
whyNot.3: Counting documents measures activity, not whether the output will cut queues.

B.q: Which statement BEST distinguishes success criteria from success factors?
options: Criteria are set by the team; factors are set by the sponsor
Criteria measure success; factors make success more likely
Criteria apply in linear projects; factors in iterative ones
Criteria are optional; factors must be agreed at the start
B.why: Success criteria are the measures used to judge success; success factors are the conditions and practices that make success more likely.

whyNot.0: Success criteria are agreed with the sponsor and stakeholders; the difference isn't who sets them.
whyNot.2: Both apply in every life cycle.
whyNot.3: Success criteria should be agreed up front; they are not optional.

B.q: Midway through a project, the business case is updated because the expected benefits have changed. What should happen to the quality indicators?
options: Leave them unchanged to keep the original baseline intact
Delete them, as the business case now replaces their role
Wait until handover, then decide whether they still fit
Review them against the new case, through change control
B.why: Indicators are derived from the business case. If it changes, they must be reviewed so quality still targets the benefits, with changes to the baseline controlled.

whyNot.0: Keeping indicators linked to old benefits means measuring the wrong thing.
whyNot.1: The business case justifies the project; it doesn't replace quality measures.
whyNot.2: Waiting until handover means outputs may be built to the wrong quality.

C.q: A council's business case for a recycling app expects higher recycling rates. The supplier proposes judging quality only by 'number of app screens delivered'. Why is this a weak quality indicator?
options: It doesn't show whether the app will deliver the benefit
It cannot be measured until after the app has gone live
It is a success factor, so it belongs in the risk register
It is too detailed to be reported to the project sponsor
C.why: A good indicator predicts the benefit. Screen count measures volume of output, not whether residents will recycle more.

whyNot.1: Screen count is easy to measure during delivery; that's not the weakness.
whyNot.2: It isn't a success factor, and success factors don't belong in the risk register.
whyNot.3: Level of detail isn't the problem; its lack of link to the benefit is.

C.q: Which is NOT a typical quality indicator?
options: Defects found per thousand lines of code
Customer satisfaction score after launch
Members on the project steering group
Proportion of units passing final inspection
C.why: The size of the steering group is a governance arrangement. It says nothing about the quality of the outputs.

whyNot.0: Defect density is a classic quality indicator.
whyNot.1: Customer satisfaction is a typical quality indicator.
whyNot.3: Inspection pass rate is a typical quality indicator.

C.q: A software team on an iterative project tracks the number of defects users report after each release. What is the MAIN advantage of tracking this indicator every iteration?
options: It removes the need to agree acceptance criteria up front
Quality trends show early, so action can be taken in time
It allows quality targets to be lowered as time runs out
It means testing can safely be left to the final iteration
C.why: Measuring every iteration gives early feedback, so problems are spotted and fixed before they build up.

whyNot.0: Criteria are still needed for each feature; the indicator doesn't replace them.
whyNot.2: In iterative projects scope flexes, not quality.
whyNot.3: Testing happens within each time box; leaving it to the end loses the benefit.

reteach.title: Running a neighbourhood café
reteach.question: You open a café because you want regulars who come back every week. Which numbers should you watch to know your coffee and service are 'good enough'?

blocks.h: Start with why the café exists
blocks.body: Your 'business case' is repeat customers. So the quality you need is whatever keeps people coming back: coffee served hot within 3 minutes, a clean table, friendly service. Watch those: average wait time, customer ratings, repeat visits. A £20,000 espresso machine might sound like 'quality', but if customers can't taste the difference, it's gold plating. The right gauges are the ones that predict the benefit you opened for.

blocks.text: A fancy machine is an input, not an indicator. Indicators measure whether the result is good enough to deliver the benefit.

explain.body: A quality indicator is a measurable sign that outputs are of the required quality. Common examples: defect rates, test pass rates, customer satisfaction, availability. If you can't measure it, it can't act as an indicator.

items.label: rate found per item or batch

test.q: Complete the statement: quality indicators are ______ signs that outputs are of the required quality.
options: subjective
optional
informal
measurable
test.why: Quality indicators must be measurable, so quality can be objectively tracked and reported.

whyNot.0: Subjective signs can't be checked objectively, so they make poor indicators.
whyNot.1: Indicators are agreed in planning and tracked; they are not optional extras.
whyNot.2: Indicators are formal, recorded measures, not informal impressions.

explain.h: The line back to the business case
explain.body: Each indicator should trace back: indicator → success criterion → benefit in the business case. That is how the business case 'defines' quality: it says which benefits matter, and the indicators show whether the outputs are good enough to deliver them.

test.q: A hospital's business case promises fewer missed appointments from a new text-reminder system. Which success criterion BEST links to this benefit?
options: Missed appointments fall by 15% within a year
The system is built using the latest technology
The project team completes all of its training
The supplier submits monthly progress reports
test.why: It measures the very benefit the business case promises, so it can judge whether the project succeeded.

whyNot.1: Latest technology is an input choice, not a measure of the benefit.
whyNot.2: Team training is a success factor, not a success criterion.
whyNot.3: Progress reporting is a governance activity, not a measure of success.

explain.body: Success criteria: the measures that judge success, agreed up front. Success factors: the conditions that make success more likely. KPIs: measures tracked during the project to show progress towards the criteria. Quality indicators often act as KPIs.

test.q: During delivery, a project manager tracks the weekly test pass rate against a target set in the plan. In this role the measure is acting as a:
options: critical success factor (CSF)
benefit realisation plan
key performance indicator
project interdependency
test.why: A measure tracked during the project against a target, to show progress towards the success criteria, is a KPI.

whyNot.0: A success factor is a condition that makes success likely, not a tracked measure.
whyNot.1: A benefits plan sets out how benefits will be realised and tracked, not a weekly test measure.
whyNot.3: An interdependency is a link between activities or projects, not a measure.

explain.body: Linear: indicators are set in definition and formally reviewed at stage ends, decision gates and final acceptance. Iterative: indicators are measured every iteration on each increment, so trends and user reactions show up early and the backlog can be re-prioritised.

test.q: In a linear project, when are quality indicators MOST likely to be formally reviewed against their targets?
options: Only once the benefits have been fully realised
At stage ends, decision gates and final acceptance
Every day, by the product owner during stand-ups
Never, as targets are fixed once the plan is baselined
test.why: Linear projects use stage ends, decision gates and acceptance as formal control points to review performance.

whyNot.0: Waiting until benefits are realised is far too late to correct quality.
whyNot.2: Daily stand-ups with a product owner are an iterative practice.
whyNot.3: Fixed targets still need reviewing to see whether they are being met.
